newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh, India agree to resolve water dispute.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh, India agree to resolve water dispute.

text.p: India and Bangladesh agreed on Saturday to end a decades-old dispute on sharing water from the mighty Ganges river.

"Water issues have been discussed at the satisfaction of Bangladesh...discussions were very productive and fruitful," Indian Foreign Minister I. K. Gujral told reporters after nearly two hours of "very productive" talks with his Bangladeshi counterpart in Dhaka.
"Political will is backing both sides. It's now a different mood," said Gujral who arrived in Bangladesh on Friday night leading a 16-member team.
Gujral, however, gave no date for signing a water-sharing agreement.
Bangladesh Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad told reporters: "We are expecting a solution by the next lean period".
"I endorse what he (Azad) is saying," Gujral said, indicating that Dhaka and Delhi expect an agreement by December.
The ministers said the size of each other's share would be determined by experts and officials at follow-up meetings soon.
Under the last agreement which expired in 1988, Bangladesh received 34,500 cusecs (cubic feet per second) of Ganges water during the dry season.
Attempts to renew the agreement have since failed, with Dhaka insisting on taking at least 80 percent of the lean-season flow.
Sharing of water from the Ganges, called Padma in Bangladesh, has long been a major irritant in relations between the two unequal south Asian neighbours.
Dhaka says India's Farakka barrage, 18 km (11 miles) from Bangladesh's northern border, obstructs the river's flow and deprives this country of its fair share of water.
Officials claim that more than 40 million people in northwestern Bangladesh have faced gradual desertification of their land since the Farakka was commissioned in 1974.
Gujral and Azad also discussed trade, repatriation of Chakma refugees from India, border security and other issues.
"We have discussed all bilateral issues...problems will be resolved," Gujral told reporters.
Up to 50,000 Chakmas fled to northeast India over the past five or six years from Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts, where troops have been fighting a fledgling tribal insurgency since 1973.
Some 6,000 Chakmas were repatriated in 1994 and several thousands more have returned on their own, officials said.
Gujral said he had not raised issues regarding New Delhi's plea for transport links through Bangladesh to northeast India at the talks.

The main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) led by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, and several fringe groups, have strongly objected to granting the transit, saying it would undermine Bangladesh's sovereignty and weaken the country's defence.
Hundreds of activists from the small Democratic League staged a black-flag protest in Dhaka on Friday ahead of Gujral's arrival, chanting: "We will give blood but not transit."
Gujral was due to meet Bangladesh's president-elect, retired chief justice Shahabuddin Ahmed, along with Commerce Minister Tofael Ahmed and Water Resources Minister Abdur Razzak later in the day.
He is to meet Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Sunday and hand her a letter from Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, Foreign Ministry officials said.
Gujral is also expected to meet Khaleda Zia before he returns home on Monday.
